http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/10/chess.text: Iran will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States meets its conditions as Iranians have shown "they are professional chess players," Tehran said on Monday.“It is up to the US side to stop and make amends for its illegal and destructive actions,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Monday, in reference to the US blockade of Iranian ports."Lights out or lights on, Iranians showed they are professional chess players," Baghaei added, in reference to US President Donald Trump likening the negotiations to a "board game".Trump on Sunday signalled he was prepared to let economic pressure mount against Iran, apparently backing away from more military strikes after Tehran issued a list of demands for opening the Strait of Hormuz.Tehran wants Washington to lift the blockade, pay compensation for months of war damage, lift economic sanctions and release Iran's frozen assets.The closure of the Strait of Hormuz — a key waterway that normally carries roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil supplies — has become the war’s most lasting consequence.The impasse has kept energy prices as a major focus of US politics ahead of November’s midterm elections.Iran is holding separate talks with Oman over transit through the strait, including potentially a temporary shipping corridor. However, Tehran said that any actual reopening is contingent on talks with the US.Trump had earlier been quoted by news outlet Axios as saying he was "low-keying it" with Iran."We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," he said."It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game," Trump added.Iranian official Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr on Saturday laid out Tehran's demands, including an end to the "war and aggression against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen and Iraq".He also demanded the lifting of a US counterblockade of Iranian ports, the end of sanctions, the release of frozen Iranian assets, and compensation for wartime damage, the Tasnim news agency reported.Baghaei on Monday reiterated that "as long as the US naval blockade continues ... the necessary conditions for saying that the Strait of Hormuz has become a safe waterway will not exist".Tehran had been engaged in negotiations with Washington on ending the war launched by the US and Israel in late February, but a preliminary deal fell apart, and its officials have said talks are now limited to exchanging messages through mediators.Khamenei meets Pezeshkian?Meanwhile, Tehran reported that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian recently met with Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared in public since assuming the post early in the war."Dr Masoud Pezeshkian met Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei and spoke with him at the start of his third year in the presidency," Khamenei's office said in a statement on Sunday, without indicating the date of the meeting.Pezeshkian, who took office in July 2024, had said in early May that he met with Khamenei, also without specifying the date, but the ayatollah's office did not issue any statements at the time.Pezeshkian had said on Wednesday that communication with Khamenei was "very difficult at the moment", and speculation has swirled about the ayatollah's health after he was reportedly wounded in strikes that killed his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.No clear indications exist on his actual whereabouts and condition, with US officials stating earlier in the war that the younger Khamenei was severely injured and likely "disfigured" in the opening salvo of the war on 28 February, while reports from inside Iran claimed he was in hiding out of precaution amid concerns over his safety.Pezeshkian, who is a medical doctor by trade, was also reported to have been at least partly in charge of his recovery, although there was no official confirmation of those claims.Mojtaba Khamenei's office said that the ayatollah and Pezeshkian "discussed in detail the country's issues and problems", including the "current military situation and future prospects".On Sunday, Tasnim news agency cited an IRGC general as saying that images showing Khamenei among the people and during meetings would be "published in the future," without offering a timeline.It is unclear how involved Khamenei might be in the ongoing negotiations with Washington, but reports have indicated that the IRGC — an elite paramilitary force of the Islamic Republic under the direct command of the ayatollah — is likely playing an outsized role in Tehran's positions and demands.Tehran touts 'change of perception' in the regionBaghaei said on Monday that a defence pact signed last week between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan was "a sign of a change in the perception" of countries in the region towards the US."The countries of the region have realised that security is not a commodity that can be bought from false brokers," Baghaei said. Washington is an ally of the three signatories to the pact."Countries in the region cannot rely on the claim of security provided by the US as in the past," he added.He also said Iran was not concerned that the pact could be aimed at Tehran, considering "deep religious, historical and civilisational ties" with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.There was "no reason to worry that this treaty will be against Iran", Baghaei said.The three nations signed the agreement on Friday against the backdrop of a five-month war between the US and Iran, which has drawn in surrounding nations and disrupted regional shipping routes.Pakistan's foreign ministry said Friday that the pact meant an attack on any member would be regarded as an attack on all, adding it was "intended to strengthen collective deterrence".

http://www.euronews.com/next/2026/08/11/.text: When Kazakhstan became one of the world's largest crypto mining hubs five years ago, the boom strained the country’s power grid, and the government’s response resulted in most miners either leaving the country or going underground.Now the Kazakh government is looking to bring it all back home by offering tax breaks and legal certainty.The Kazakh government signed a decree designed to encourage citizens to declare cryptocurrency holdings, move them onto regulated domestic platforms and integrate digital assets into the country's economy.The authorities are offering private investors a tax break on personal income from digital asset transactions for three years, provided the assets were not connected to fraud, money laundering or linked to unlicensed crypto services.The decision has opened the door to making it easier for miners to operate in the country — and for everyone to profit.Crypto boom cut shortCryptocurrency mining uses powerful computers to solve complex mathematical problems in order to verify and add transactions to a blockchain — the ledger on which a cryptocurrency's transaction history is recorded.Miners who successfully complete them are rewarded with cryptocurrency deposited directly to their personal crypto wallets, which in some cases like Bitcoin can bring in significant profits.The downside is that the process consumes a large amount of power because the computations require sustained processing.After China banned Bitcoin mining in 2021, many miners began looking for new locations with low-cost energy.At that point Kazakhstan rapidly became the second-largest Bitcoin mining location after the US. Many tried to get in on the profits, with people even putting mining equipment on their balconies.Some went so far as to masquerade the mining farms as vegetable storage facilities, greenhouses or AI data centres at abandoned Soviet-era industrial sites to conceal their massive electricity consumption.The country did not get to enjoy the crypto bloom for too long. The rapid influx of miners placed an enormous burden on the country’s ageing electricity grid.In October 2021, surging electricity demand contributed to outages at three power plants in northeastern Kazakhstan, while rolling blackouts affected several regions. At peak, cryptocurrency miners were consuming an estimated 8% of Kazakhstan's total electricity output.Authorities responded by repeatedly tightening regulations on electricity consumption and digital asset legalisation, leading to miners' departure abroad and the proliferation of illegal operations.Kazakhstan never outright banned crypto mining, keeping its options open to potentially harness its potential in the future.According to Kazakhstan's financial regulator, Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), Kazakh citizens own approximately 1 million crypto wallets.The AIFC, modelled on Dubai's DIFC financial free zone, has functioned as Kazakhstan's sandbox for financial innovation and serves as the regulatory home for digital asset companies operating in the country.This figure is nearly four times the number of users registered on authorised local exchanges, which in March reached 256,900.Bringing crypto assets back onshoreAttracting crypto owners back to their home countries with incentives and simplified legal frameworks has turned into a global trend in recent years, experts say.The UAE, Hong Kong and Singapore have implemented similar tax measures alongside clear licensing, regulations and access to banking services, bringing in additional revenue.The decree also addresses the energy question that triggered Kazakhstan's earlier mining crisis.Under the plan, associated gas from oil fields not required for state use can be used to generate electricity for mining operations, broadening miners' options beyond the main national grid.General Manager of Binance Kazakhstan Nurkhat Kushimov believes the tax incentive is the most important measure in the decree.“This is a strong incentive for users to choose regulated jurisdictions and platforms operating within them," Kushimov told Euronews."This approach makes working in a licensed environment more attractive, fosters trust in the market and creates the conditions for its further development,” he said.Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Association of Fintech, AI and Crypto Industry Bakhytzhan Kenzhebayev believes that the tax incentive removes one of the main uncertainties for the private investor, namely the question of when and on what basis the obligation arises. But the measure in itself is not sufficient.“Users choose a platform not based on the tax rate, but on a combination of factors: how easy it is to deposit and withdraw (the local currency), the liquidity, and how clear the rules are,” Kenzhebayev told Euronews."For a licensed participant, the predictability of the rule is more valuable than the benefit itself."President of Kazakhstan’s Blockchain and Digital Mining Association Daniyar Mubarakov told Euronews that any government support is welcome, but wonders how long this measure will work.“For certain categories of entrepreneurs preferential tax regimes mean not only a reduction in taxes in the current period, but also a possible several-fold increase in taxes in the future due to increased volumes,” Mubarakov said.Vice Minister of AI and Digital Development Gizzat Baitursynov said that his department is working on a proposal for a simplified tax regime following the expiration of the exemption in three years' time.He added that the department is also working on cancelling tax audits for private investors covering the previous three years.Beyond tax incentivesExperts say that Kazakh private investors' return to domestic platforms will depend on their competitiveness.“For most users, convenience of service, liquidity, availability of instruments, speed of transactions, and the ability to seamlessly interact with the banking system remain the key factors,” Kushimov said.According to Kenzhebayev, the main risks now lie in the legal definitions and terminology used. If the exemption is defined too broadly, it could create space to abuse the system and avoid paying taxes on other assets unrelated to crypto.“This creates the risk of a reversal of the norm in a year or two, and that causes more damage to the market than an initially high but stable rate,” Kenzhebayev explained.He also warned that the same digital asset can be treated as two different things depending on whether it falls under the AIFC or Kazakhstan's national rules, which would in turn mean companies would have to comply with two separate legal structures at once."The difficulty arises at the intersection. As a result, the participant builds two parallel infrastructures for one business, which reflects on the costs," he said.Kenzhebayev said tax breaks alone would not be enough to draw users to licensed Kazakh platforms.What would make the difference, he said, is reliable access to banking, clear rules for converting crypto into the local currency, straightforward requirements for keeping client assets safe, and a regulatory environment that does not put licensed operators at a disadvantage.

https://www.baltictimes.com/lithuanian_p.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Lithuanian PM criticises airport board appointment over alleged Russia, Belarus ties 2026-08-21 BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius on Friday called the appointment of independent board member Oleksandras Laneckis to state-owned Lithuanian Airports "unpleasant", after activists and politicians raised concerns over his alleged past ties to Russia and Belarus. However, Sinkevicius said he did not hold Transport Minister Juras Taminskas responsible for the situation. "As I understand it, the member himself has resigned, and the matter is effectively closed. But let us look at the entire board appointment process. There are selection committees. It is not as if the minister himself collects CVs and makes a choice. If that were the case, we could raise questions. But there are recruitment agencies and numerous people who evaluate qualifications and compliance, and something may have failed here. It appears that the candidate profiles did not reveal what individual public figures later managed to identify," the prime minister told reporters on Friday. "It is an unpleasant case; I hope it will not be repeated and that we will look more responsibly at board member selections in the future," Sinkevicius added. On Thursday, Taminskas removed Laneckis from the new Lithuanian Airports board at his own request. Laneckis said that while he disagreed with the issues raised publicly, he did not wish to hinder the operations of Lithuanian Airports. Taminskas had previously asked the State Security Department to urgently conduct an additional security clearance assessment for Laneckis. The minister said he was unaware of the circumstances regarding Laneckis's activities that had been disclosed publicly. The opposition Conservatives had questioned whether Laneckis's role on the Lithuanian Airports board was aligned with Lithuania's national security interests. According to the opposition, Laneckis continues to give interviews and commentary to pro-Russian media and publishes articles on how to bypass Western sanctions. Laneckis was intended to be responsible for strategic planning and aviation on the Lithuanian Airports board. Comments Related Articles Subscribe Log In Ads Please enter your username and password.
